questions.q: Which region of a running program's memory does Valgrind's Memcheck tool primarily check for errors?
choices: Heap memory allocated with malloc() and released with free()
Global data memory
The read-only code (text) segment
CPU registers
questions.explain: Memcheck highlights heap memory errors. The heap is the memory a program allocates dynamically with malloc() and releases with free().

questions.q: Which of the following kinds of errors can Valgrind's Memcheck detect?
choices: Reading a value from uninitialized heap memory
Reading or writing at an unallocated heap location (e.g., array out-of-bounds)
Freeing memory that was already freed
Memory leaks
Out-of-bounds accesses to a global array
questions.explain: Memcheck finds uninitialized reads, invalid reads and writes, double frees, and leaks in heap memory. It does not detect memory access errors in global data memory.

choices: Reading from uninitialized memory
Writing to unallocated memory
Freeing already freed memory
A memory leak
questions.explain: ptr[3] is inside the allocated block, but nothing was ever stored there, so the code reads an uninitialized value.

choices: A memory leak of the first block of 10 ints
A double free
Reading from uninitialized memory
Writing to unallocated memory
questions.explain: Reassigning ptr loses the only address of the first block. Nothing refers to that block anymore, so it can never be freed.

choices: Freeing already freed memory
A memory leak
Reading from uninitialized memory
Nothing; the second call to free() is ignored
questions.explain: The second call frees the same pointer again, so it frees memory that was already freed.

questions.q: What do you call a chunk of allocated heap memory that no pointer variable in the program refers to anymore, so it can never be freed?
questions.explain: A memory leak happens when a program loses the address of an allocated chunk of heap space.

questions.q: After ptr = malloc(sizeof(int) * 10);, the statement ptr[10] = 100; writes to valid, allocated memory.
questions.explain: The block holds 10 ints at indices 0 through 9. Index 10 is past the end, so this writes to unallocated memory.

questions.q: What can happen if a program keeps leaking memory?
choices: It can run out of heap space, and later calls to malloc() fail
The compiler refuses to build the program
free() starts freeing the wrong blocks automatically
The leaked memory is moved to the stack
questions.explain: Leaks can eventually use up the heap, and then later calls to malloc() fail.

questions.q: Why are memory access errors often hard to find and fix?
choices: They often don't cause a visible error right away; the symptom shows up later in execution
The symptom may appear in a part of the program that seems unrelated to the actual bug
The program may run correctly on some inputs and crash on others
The compiler reports them only as warnings, which are easy to miss
questions.explain: Memory errors often show up later, in seemingly unrelated code, and only on some inputs. The compiler does not detect them, which is why runtime tools like Valgrind are useful.

questions.q: A program that runs fine on some inputs but crashes on others may have a memory access error.
questions.explain: Behavior that changes with input, such as working on some inputs and crashing on others, is a classic sign of a memory access error.

questions.q: An invalid write to heap memory always crashes the program immediately, on the line that does the bad write.
questions.explain: Invalid writes often have no immediate effect. They may corrupt other data and cause a crash later, or never visibly affect a run at all.

questions.q: In a large program, a heap write overruns one variable's block and corrupts another variable's data. What is usually the only connection between the two variables?
choices: Their memory happens to be allocated close together in the heap
They have the same type
They are declared in the same function
One is a pointer to the other
questions.explain: There may be no logical link between them. They are connected only because their memory addresses sit near each other in the heap, and that layout can change from run to run.

choices: 11 and 12 only
Only 13
None; the loop stays in bounds
questions.explain: The valid indices are 0 through 9. The loop runs up to i = 12, so it writes three indices past the end: 10, 11, and 12.

questions.q: bigfish holds 10 ints. How many out-of-bounds writes does for (i = 0; i < 13; i++) bigfish[i] = 66 + i; perform?
questions.explain: The loop writes indices 0 through 12, which is 13 writes. Only 10 of them are in bounds, so 3 are out of bounds.

questions.q: In the bigfish program, the loop for (i = 0; i < 13; i++) bigfish[i] = 66 + i; runs, and afterward littlefish[0] prints as 78 instead of 0. Which index of bigfish was written with the value 78?
questions.explain: 66 + i = 78 gives i = 12. The out-of-bounds write to bigfish[12] landed on the memory of littlefish[0].

questions.q: In the bigfish program, out-of-bounds writes to bigfish happen in a loop, but the program crashes later at free(littlefish). What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The writes overwrote heap metadata that malloc() stores just before littlefish's block, and free() uses that metadata to decide how much memory to free
littlefish was never allocated, so freeing it crashes
free() checks whether array values are in range and rejects littlefish
bigfish was freed first, so littlefish became invalid
questions.explain: malloc() can store metadata in the heap right before each allocated block. Overwriting the metadata for littlefish corrupts the information free() relies on, so the crash shows up at free(littlefish).

questions.q: GDB shows the bigfish program crashing at free(littlefish), so the bug must be in how the program accesses littlefish.
questions.explain: The crash happens at free(littlefish), but the cause is the out-of-bounds writes to bigfish. The program never accesses littlefish incorrectly.

questions.q: Every malloc() implementation stores its bookkeeping metadata in the heap immediately before each allocated block.
questions.explain: Some implementations do this, but not all of them use this strategy.

questions.q:
Valgrind reports this for the bigfish program:

Invalid write
 at main (bigfish.c:27)
 Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 40 alloc'd
   by main (bigfish.c:11)

What does the "block of size 40" allocated at line 11 refer to?
choices: The bigfish array: 10 ints of 4 bytes each
An array of 40 ints
The littlefish array
40 bytes of malloc metadata
questions.explain: Line 11 is bigfish = malloc(sizeof(int) * 10), which with 4-byte ints is 40 bytes. The invalid write lands right after the end of that block.

questions.q: Which changes would fix the out-of-bounds write in the bigfish program?
choices: Pass more bytes to malloc() when allocating bigfish
Change the loop bounds so the loop stops writing at index 9
Remove the call to free(littlefish)
Allocate littlefish before bigfish
questions.explain: The fix is to make the allocation big enough or keep the loop within the existing allocation. Removing free() or reordering the mallocs only hides the symptom.

questions.q: Every line of Valgrind output starts with a prefix such as ==31059==. What is 31059?
choices: The process ID (PID) of the program being run
The number of errors found
The memory address of the error
The source line number of the error
questions.explain: Valgrind starts each line of output with the process's ID number.

questions.q: Most Valgrind error messages have three parts: the type of error, a stack trace of where the error happened, and what else?
choices: Where the heap memory near the error was allocated
The values of all local variables
The suggested fix for the error
The number of bytes of heap memory still in use
questions.explain: The third part shows where the heap memory around the error was allocated, which is usually the allocation involved in the error.

questions.q:
Valgrind output:

==31059== Invalid write of size 1
==31059==    at 0x4006C5: foo (valgrindbadprog.c:29)
==31059==    by 0x40079A: main (valgrindbadprog.c:56)
==31059==  Address 0x52045c5 is 0 bytes after a block of size 5 alloc'd
==31059==    at 0x4C2DB8F: malloc (in /usr/lib/valgrind/...)
==31059==    by 0x400660: foo (valgrindbadprog.c:18)
==31059==    by 0x40079A: main (valgrindbadprog.c:56)

On which source line did the invalid write happen?
questions.explain: The top line of the stack trace, at foo (valgrindbadprog.c:29), shows where the error happened.

questions.q:
Valgrind output:

==31059== Invalid write of size 1
==31059==    at 0x4006C5: foo (valgrindbadprog.c:29)
==31059==    by 0x40079A: main (valgrindbadprog.c:56)
==31059==  Address 0x52045c5 is 0 bytes after a block of size 5 alloc'd
==31059==    at 0x4C2DB8F: malloc (in /usr/lib/valgrind/...)
==31059==    by 0x400660: foo (valgrindbadprog.c:18)
==31059==    by 0x40079A: main (valgrindbadprog.c:56)

On which source line was the heap block near the bad write allocated?
questions.explain: In the allocation section, the call to malloc() was made by foo at valgrindbadprog.c:18.

questions.q: In a Valgrind stack trace, what does the line "by 0x40079A: main (valgrindbadprog.c:56)" under "at 0x4006C5: foo (valgrindbadprog.c:29)" tell you?
choices: foo() was called from main() at line 56
main() was called from foo() at line 56
A second, separate error happened at line 56
Line 56 allocated the memory involved in the error
questions.explain: The trace lists the function where the error happened first, followed by its callers. The error was in foo() at line 29, and main() called foo() at line 56.

questions.q: What does "Address 0x52045c5 is 0 bytes after a block of size 5 alloc'd" mean?
choices: The bad access was to the byte right after the end of a 5-byte heap block
The access was 5 bytes past the end of a block
The program allocated a 0-byte block
The address is 5 bytes before the start of a block
questions.explain: "0 bytes after" means the access is right past the last valid byte of the 5-byte block. This is a typical off-by-one overrun.

choices: The loop runs one time too many and writes c[5], which is past the end of c
str was never allocated
c should be cast to int * instead of char *
The loop never writes c[0]
questions.explain: c holds 5 chars at indices 0 through 4. With i <= 5 the loop also writes c[5]. To fix it, change the loop bounds or allocate a larger array.

questions.q: Which gcc flag adds debugging information to the executable before you run it under Valgrind?
choices: -g
-Wall
-c
questions.explain: Compile with -g (e.g., gcc -g valgrindbadprog.c) so the executable includes debugging information.

questions.q: If you run valgrind ./a.out without naming a tool, Valgrind runs Memcheck.
questions.explain: Memcheck is Valgrind's default tool.

questions.q: Which Valgrind command-line option explicitly selects the Memcheck tool?
questions.explain: --tool=memcheck selects Memcheck. The --tool option also selects Valgrind's other tools.

questions.q: Which Valgrind option shows details about each individual memory leak?
questions.explain: --leak-check=yes shows details about individual memory leaks.

questions.q: When does Memcheck report memory access errors, and when does it report its memory leak summary?
choices: Errors as they occur during execution; the leak summary at the end of execution
Both only at the end of execution
Both as they occur during execution
The leak summary first, then errors after the program exits
questions.explain: Memcheck prints errors and warnings as they occur, then prints a summary of memory leaks when the program finishes.

questions.q: Valgrind reports both invalid reads/writes and memory leaks. Which should you usually fix first?
choices: The invalid reads/writes and other access errors, unless leaks are making the program run out of heap memory
Memory leaks, because they are always the root cause
Whichever appears last in the output
Neither; Valgrind warnings are usually false positives
questions.explain: Leaks matter, but the other memory access errors are much more critical to correctness. Fix those first, unless leaks are making the program run out of heap space and crash.

questions.q: For a non-interactive program, which command saves both Valgrind's output and the program's output to output.txt?
choices: valgrind -v ./a.out >& output.txt
valgrind -v ./a.out < output.txt
valgrind -v output.txt ./a.out
gcc -g ./a.out > output.txt
questions.explain: >& sends both standard output and standard error (where Valgrind writes its messages) to the file, which you can read after the program exits.

questions.q: The code around a Valgrind error doesn't make the cause clear. What is a good next step?
choices: Use GDB with breakpoints near the reported lines to inspect the program's runtime state
Recompile without -g and run Valgrind again
Ignore the error if the program's output looks correct
Add more calls to free() at the end of main()
questions.explain: Valgrind shows where the error is, and GDB shows the runtime state there. For example, a breakpoint at line 29 that prints i shows the out-of-bounds access when i is 5.

questions.q: Valgrind detects memory access errors involving global data memory.
questions.explain: Valgrind does not detect memory access errors in global data memory.

questions.q: Valgrind detects stack memory errors in as much detail as heap memory errors.
questions.explain: Valgrind can find some stack errors, such as uninitialized local variables or accesses beyond the bounds of the current stack, but not in as much detail as heap errors.

questions.q: What can happen if a program writes past the end of an array declared statically on the stack?
choices: Other local variables change value "mysteriously"
Saved state used to return from a function call is overwritten, crashing the program when the function returns
Valgrind always reports the exact array and index involved
The compiler automatically grows the array
questions.explain: Stack overruns can corrupt nearby locals or the saved return state, causing a crash at function return. Valgrind may not catch these errors.

questions.q: Which Valgrind tool profiles cache behavior?
choices: Cachegrind
Callgrind
Massif
Memcheck
questions.explain: Cachegrind profiles cache behavior. Callgrind profiles code, Massif profiles memory use, and Memcheck finds memory errors.
